inline.s: The Buddha told Subhūti: Subhūti! They are not sentient beings, and yet they are not entirely non-sentient beings either. Why is that? Subhūti! Because sentient beings are but illusions (these sentient beings, as the Tathāgata declares, are not sentient beings, and so are merely called sentient beings), while their intrinsic nature is the same as the Buddha’s—omniscient and all-capable—and so they are fully able to give rise to faith in this.
[Sentient beings, sentient beings]—through this repetition, spoken in an emphatic tone, it carries forward the passage above: “They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings.”

blocks.text: Section 22: Nothing Attainable in the Dharma

inline.s: The preceding section said that the Tathāgata has no Dharma to teach; this section speaks of how the Tathāgata has no Dharma to attain.
[Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! When the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was there truly nothing attained?]
Subhūti respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! When the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was it truly a matter of having nothing attained?
[The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhūti! With regard to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have not even the slightest Dharma to attain, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

The Buddha replied: So it is, so it is. Subhūti! Not only do I have nothing attained with respect to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, but I have not even the slightest Dharma to attain. Having completely departed from all marks, this is what is called the supreme, perfect enlightenment.

See Section Seven, “Nothing Attained, Nothing Taught”: “Subhūti! What do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Does the Tathāgata have any Dharma to teach?” Subhūti said: “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, there is no fixed Dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; nor is there any fixed Dharma that the Tathāgata can teach.” And Section Seventeen, “Without an Ultimate Self”: “Subhūti! What do you think? When the Tathāgata was at the abode of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there any Dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?” “No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, when the Buddha was at the abode of Dīpaṃkara, there was no Dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is. Subhūti! There truly is no Dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti! If there were a Dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’ Since there is truly no Dharma by which anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is attained, therefore Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’ Why is that? The Tathāgata is precisely the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. If anyone says that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Subhūti! There truly is no Dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata lies within neither the real nor the unreal.’”

The cultivation that is no cultivation, and the realization that is no realization, hold two levels of meaning: First, why should one cultivate and realize? The purpose is to awaken from the dream of ignorance. Therefore one must cultivate while detached from marks and realize while detached from marks in order to escape illusion; thus, cultivation without cultivating and realization without realizing are the correct path. Second, at the fundamental level, cultivation and realization are both matters within the dream of ignorance—there is no truly existing cultivation or realization—and so it is said that there is no cultivation and no realization. Even so, one must still cultivate and realize in order to awaken from the dream of ignorance, but one must always cultivate while detached from marks and realize while detached from marks.
That the World-Honored One taught no Dharma and attained no anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is truly hard to believe, and so the sutra repeatedly returns to these two matters.

When speaking of how all dharmas are like a dream or an illusion, Great Master Hanshan said: “All Buddhas manifest through the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate through the power of illusion; all two-vehicle practitioners seek stillness through the power of illusion; all externalists are deluded through the power of illusion; all sentient beings pass through birth and death through the power of illusion. Even heavenly palaces and the Pure Land are established through the power of illusion; jade groves and jeweled trees flourish through the power of illusion; iron beds and copper pillars are arrayed through the power of illusion; the boiling cauldron and burning coals rage through the power of illusion; those with scales, shells, and feathers fly and dive through the power of illusion; the creeping, writhing, wriggling creatures rest and move through the power of illusion. That which all Buddhas of the three times have realized and which the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted—all of it never leaves this net of illusion.’ (See Mengyou ji
the instruction to the Chan practitioner Zhenyu’)

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, those bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the final age who, by cultivating and practicing this mind, attain accomplishment—for them there is here neither cultivation nor accomplishment; the perfect enlightenment shines universally, still and extinct, without duality. Within it, the Buddhalands of hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeyas, ineffable as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, rising and vanishing in confusion—neither apart from nor attached to anything, neither bound nor freed. Then for the first time one knows that sentient beings originally are Buddhas, and that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night.”

Great Master Hanshan commented: This re-explains the characteristic of perfect enlightenment universally shining, still and extinct, without duality, in order to reveal the ultimate realization of the one mind. For within the tathāgatagarbha there are originally no marks of delusion or awakening, birth-and-death or coming-and-going. Yet birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are all matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance has been broken, when one looks back upon past events it is but a dream of last night.

blocks.text: Section 23: Purifying the Mind and Practicing Good

inline.s: A pure mind is a mind of purity free of discrimination and attachment. The sutra passage of this section says: “With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, practice all wholesome dharmas, and one then attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Hence this section is titled: Purifying the Mind and Practicing Good.

[Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal and impartial, with no high or low, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, if one practices all wholesome dharmas, then one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]
Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal and impartial, with no high or low, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

—Moreover, Subhūti! This Dharma (referring to the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi spoken of above) regards all things equally, for having truly realized that these are all illusions, there arise no discriminations of high or low, noble or base, right or wrong, defiled or pure; and so this is called the supreme, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Tang
Xuanzang’s translation: “Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal, and within it there is nothing that is not equal; therefore it is called the supreme, perfect enlightenment.”

This passage says: What is supreme, perfect enlightenment? Supreme, perfect enlightenment is the complete casting away of all discriminations and attachments—this is the Buddha, and this is the Dharma attained by the Buddha.
This Dharma is equal and impartial, with no high or low, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”—this carries several meanings:
1. Any sentient being can realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

2. No matter what path is taken, and no matter whether the time be short or long, so long as one fully awakens, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For those who realize it, there is no high or low, no old or new, no shallow or deep.
3. The Dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi regards all things equally.
Why do we discriminate and cling? Because we take illusions to be real! Therefore we cling to marks and grasp at circumstances, and so there is transmigration.

The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Those who study the Way today, if they do not awaken within their own minds, but instead, beyond the mind, cling to marks and grasp at circumstances, all of this is against the Way. As for the sand of the Ganges, the Buddha says it is sand. When Buddhas and bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas walk over it, the sand is not pleased; when oxen, sheep, insects, and ants trample upon it, the sand is not angered; when precious treasures and sweet fragrances are laid upon it, the sand is not greedy; when excrement and filth are cast upon it, the sand is not repulsed. This mind is the mind of no-mind (not grasping at marks, regarding all things equally). Apart from all marks, sentient beings and Buddhas are no longer different; if only one can be without mind (without discriminating or clinging), that is the ultimate. Those who study the Way, if they do not directly become without mind, though they cultivate for countless kalpas, they will ultimately never accomplish the Way, being bound by the meritorious practices of the three vehicles and unable to gain liberation.”

[Three vehicles] “Vehicle” (yāna) means a means of conveyance; here it is a metaphor for the Dharma-gate that carries sentient beings across birth-and-death to the far shore of nirvāṇa. In accordance with the dull, middling, and sharp faculties of sentient beings, the Buddha spoke three kinds of doctrine: the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle. The three vehicles are: the lesser vehicle, the middling vehicle, and the great vehicle. The lesser vehicle is the śrāvaka vehicle, the middling vehicle is the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the great vehicle is the bodhisattva vehicle.

In this sutra the World-Honored One, with earnest and repeated instruction, simply wants us to awaken from our deluded dreams and cease discriminating and clinging. Love and hate, grasping and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion, and pride are the root of birth-and-death; they must be eradicated before one can put an end to birth-and-death. Therefore one must exert great effort in removing discrimination and clinging from the mind.
The “no-direction verse” of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
If one truly cultivates the Way, he sees not the faults of the world;
If he sees the faults of others, his own faulting is the greater wrong;
Others may be at fault, but I shall not be at fault; my own faulting is itself a fault;
Only do away with this fault-finding mind, and strike down and shatter affliction;
When love and hate no longer touch the heart, stretch out both feet and lie down.

[Love and hate no longer touch the heart] This means that feelings of love and hate no longer arise in the mind. Where sentient beings are deluded, they are deluded by clinging to marks and grasping at circumstances, vainly discriminating.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, because of the accomplishment of enlightenment, you should know that the bodhisattva is not bound by dharmas and does not seek release from dharmas; does not loathe birth-and-death and does not love nirvāṇa; does not revere those who uphold the precepts and does not hate those who break them; does not esteem long practice and does not slight beginners. Why is that? Because all is enlightened. For example, when the light of the eye discerns the scene before it, its illumination being complete, there is no love or hate. Why is that? Because the essence of light is non-dual, and so there is no love or hate.”

Great Master Hanshan commented: This reveals the one mind, still and extinct, equal and non-dual, precisely displaying the characteristic of pure enlightenment. For bondage and liberation, love and hate, and so forth are all dual characteristics; because of the deluded views of ignorance, there are dual characteristics. Now, through universal illumination, all is enlightened, and therefore there is no duality. The light of the eye is the universal illumination of direct perception of the eight consciousnesses; among all the sense faculties the eye is the most manifest, and so it is used as a metaphor for the non-dual essence of perfect enlightenment universally shining.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, all obstructions are the ultimate enlightenment. Gaining mindfulness and losing mindfulness are no other than liberation. The dharma accomplished and the dharma destroyed are both called nirvāṇa. Wisdom and ignorance are alike prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and by externalists are equally bodhi. Ignorance and true thusness are not different realms. The precepts, samādhi, and wisdom, along with lust, anger, and delusion—all are pure conduct. Sentient beings and lands share the same dharma nature. Hells and heavenly palaces are all the Pure Land. Those with nature and those without nature alike accomplish the Buddha Way. All afflictions are ultimately liberated. The sea of wisdom of the dharma realm, illumining all marks, is like the sky. This is called the Tathāgata’s accordant enlightenment nature.”

Great Master Hanshan commented: This “ultimate” serves to display the equal Buddha-wisdom. The ten pairs—gaining mindfulness and losing mindfulness, and so on—are all matters on the side of delusion and awakening. For the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment does not belong to the paired causality of delusion and awakening; everything is still, extinct, equal, and one. Seen through false views, there are dual characteristics; but if illumined by the sea-wisdom of the dharma realm, it is like the sky, and all marks are utterly ungraspable. (See Great Master Hanshan’s Straight Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment.)
The Song of Realizing the Way says: “In the dream, the six realms are clearly present; after awakening, all is empty—no trichiliocosm.”
With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, if one practices all wholesome dharmas, then one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

—Then how does one realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? The World-Honored One said: With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, by practicing any wholesome dharma, one can realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan”—that is, realizing that all marks are illusory, with nothing to seek and nothing to cling to.

This says that the key to realizing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the absence of the four marks, not the kind of wholesome dharma one practices. The wholesome dharma practiced without the four marks is the unconditioned dharma. Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the universal principle for realizing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; from this one also knows how crucial it is to be free of the four marks! How very important!
[Wholesome dharmas] The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

the third chapter, “The Chapter on Practicing and Responding,” says: “What are wholesome dharmas? They are: the ten courses of wholesome action, the five precepts, the eight-fold observance of full attainment (that is, the eight precepts), the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless concentrations, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four psychic faculties, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.” Because bodhisattvas originally attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through practicing the six perfections, the six perfections are not enumerated in the wholesome dharmas above.
[Subhūti! As for the wholesome dharmas of which I speak, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas, and so they are called wholesome dharmas.]
Subhūti! As for the so-called wholesome dharmas (having marks), the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas (without essence), and so they are called wholesome dharmas (being illusion).

This says that wholesome dharmas are illusory. To prevent sentient beings from again clinging to marks with respect to wholesome dharmas, the World-Honored One earnestly admonished: Wholesome dharmas are illusions, and therefore one must be detached from marks and practice wholesome dharmas with a pure mind.
Those who uphold, read, and recite this sutra and expound it for others—their merit is incomparable, and their wisdom is likewise incomparable; hence it is called “Incomparable Merit and Wisdom.”

[Subhūti! If in the trichiliocosm all the kings of Mount Sumeru, and masses of the seven treasures such as these, were gathered up and someone used them in giving; and if another person upheld, read, and recited this Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, even a four-line verse, and expounded it for others—the merit of the former would not equal one hundredth of the latter, nor one hundred thousand myriad billionth of it, nor could it be reached by reckoning or simile.]

Subhūti! If someone, with the volume of all the kings of Mount Sumeru in the trichiliocosm, were to fill it with the seven treasures and give as a gift; and if another person were to uphold, read, and recite this Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, even a four-line verse, and expound it for others—the merit of the former would not equal one hundredth of the latter, nor one hundred thousand myriad billionth of it, nor even a fraction of that vast number which no reckoning or simile can describe.

After the World-Honored One had spoken of wholesome dharmas as illusion (“Subhūti! As for the wholesome dharmas of which I speak, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas, and so they are called wholesome dharmas”), he next spoke of the incomparable merit of those who uphold, read, and recite this sutra and expound it for others—lest some fall into the extreme of denying dharmas.
Transforming without transformation’ means that the Tathāgata delivers and transforms sentient beings while detached from marks.

[Subhūti! What do you think? Do not suppose that the Tathāgata conceives the thought, “I shall save sentient beings.” Subhūti! Do not hold such a thought. Why is that? Because in truth there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves. If there were sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves, then the Tathāgata would have a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan.]

Subhūti! What do you think? Do not suppose that the Tathāgata conceives such a thought: “I shall save sentient beings.” Subhūti! Do not think like this. Why is that? Because there is truly no such matter as the Tathāgata saving sentient beings. If the Tathāgata were to think that there is such a matter as the Tathāgata saving sentient beings, then the Tathāgata would have the marks of self, person, sentient being, and lifespan.

[In truth there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves] There is truly no such matter as the Tathāgata saving sentient beings. This says that the Tathāgata’s saving of sentient beings is also an illusion, because “all marks are false and unreal.” When reading the Diamond Sutra, one should note that many passages are expositions of the line “All marks are false and unreal.”

[Subhūti! The Tathāgata, in speaking of a self, says there is no self; yet ordinary people imagine that there is a self. Subhūti! As for ordinary people, the Tathāgata says they are not ordinary people, and so they are called ordinary people.]

Subhūti! The Tathāgata speaks of a self in order to deliver and transform sentient beings, and this “self” spoken of by the Tathāgata is an illusion; yet ordinary people imagine that the “self” truly exists. Subhūti! This “self” is an illusion, and moreover these ordinary people who imagine that “the self truly exists” are also illusions—ordinary people (having marks), as the Tathāgata says, are not ordinary people (without essence), and so they are called ordinary people (being illusion).
[Ordinary people] Sentient beings within the three realms.

blocks.text: Section 26: The Dharmakāya Is Without Marks

inline.s: The dharmakāya is without marks’ means that the dharmakāya is without marks and cannot be seen by them. The Mahāyāna Homogeneous Sutra says: “The Tathāgata’s true dharmakāya is without color, without manifestation, without attachment, invisible, without speech, without abode, without marks, without retribution, without birth, without extinction, without simile.”
[Dharmakāya] One of the Buddha’s three bodies (dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya); it is the body of true thusness realized by all Buddhas.
[Subhūti! What do you think—can one contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti said: So it is! So it is! One can contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.]
Subhūti! What do you think—is one who has the thirty-two marks the Tathāgata? Subhūti replied: So it is, so it is. One can contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.
[Contemplate] The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra (Jingying) says: “To contemplate means to bind the mind in thoughtful examination; this is called contemplation.”

In section thirteen, the question was whether one “sees” the Tathāgata: “Subhūti, what do you think—can one see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is that? The Tathāgata says the thirty-two marks are non-marks, and so they are called the thirty-two marks.” Subhūti answered: “One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.” (Because the thirty-two marks are illusory.)
Here the World-Honored One asks: Can one “contemplate” the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied: So it is, so it is. One can contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.
This answer is wrong, and so in what follows the World-Honored One corrects it.

[The Buddha said: Subhūti! If one contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a cakravartin (wheel-turning sage king) would be the Tathāgata. Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, one should not contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.]

Subhūti! If one thinks that whoever possesses the thirty-two marks is the Tathāgata, then a cakravartin would be the Tathāgata, for the cakravartin also possesses the thirty-two marks. Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, one should not think that whoever possesses the thirty-two marks is the Tathāgata.

[Cakravartin sage king] Also called simply a cakravartin, or wheel-turning king, he is the most blessed person in the world, appearing in an age when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, and he governs the four continents. He enjoys four kinds of karmic reward: First, great wealth—treasures, goods, fields, and dwellings are numerous, the greatest in the world; second, a solemn and upright appearance possessing the thirty-two marks; third, a healthy body free of illness, peaceful and happy; fourth, a long lifespan, the greatest in the world. When a cakravartin appears, the world is at peace, the people are happy, and there are no natural calamities or human misfortunes. This results from much cultivation of merit in past lives; but regrettably, without cultivating the wisdom that transcends the world, he becomes merely a blessed great king ruling the world, and cannot cultivate, awaken to the Way, and realize the fruit.
[At that time the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
If one seeks to see me through form, or seeks me through sound,
that person treads a false path and cannot see the Tathāgata.]
At this the World-Honored One spoke in verse: If anyone vainly seeks to see me through form, or seeks me through sound, that person treads a false path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

Both the body of form and sound are illusions; one cannot see the Tathāgata through them. If anyone seeks to see the Tathāgata through the body of form and sound, that path is wrong, and one cannot see the Tathāgata. Then how can one see the Tathāgata? This is what section five says: “If one sees that all marks are not marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.”

Neither annihilation nor extinction’ means that one must not cling to the view of annihilation. Above, the World-Honored One, all the while breaking attachments, repeatedly clarified that dharmas are not truly existing; yet, fearing that sentient beings might fall into the other extreme—thinking that dharmas are wholly nonexistent, even denying that marks exist—he admonishes in this section: “Those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation with regard to dharmas.”

[Subhūti! If you think thus—the Tathāgata, because he does not have the complete marks, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti! Do not think thus—the Tathāgata, because he does not have the complete marks, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

Subhūti! If you think thus—the Tathāgata, without needing the complete marks, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (supreme, perfect enlightenment). Subhūti! Do not think thus—the Tathāgata, without needing the complete marks, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[The complete marks] These are the “complete marks” spoken of earlier. The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty minor characteristics, and so he is said to have the complete marks.

The preceding section said that the thirty-two marks are illusory and cannot be used to contemplate the Tathāgata. To prevent his listeners from falling into annihilation, the World-Honored One next admonishes: “Do not think thus—the Tathāgata, because he does not have the complete marks, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

In section twenty there is this passage: “Subhūti! What do you think—can the Tathāgata be seen by the complete marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata should not be seen by the complete marks. Why is that? The Tathāgata says the complete marks are not complete, and so they are called the complete marks.”
Now the World-Honored One tells Subhūti: Do not negate the phenomenal fact that “the Tathāgata must have the complete marks in order to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

[Subhūti! If you think thus—those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi speak of the annihilation of dharmas. Do not think thus! Why is that? Those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation with regard to dharmas.]

Subhūti! If you think thus—the Tathāgata, without needing the complete marks, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—that is, if you negate the phenomenal fact that “the Tathāgata must have the complete marks in order to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” then you are negating that marks exist, and that is a vain clinging to the view of annihilation. Those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should not hold such a wrong view.

[Annihilation] The denial of everything. The view of annihilation, also called the nihilist view, is the most evil among wrong views, and is extremely harmful. [Speaking of the annihilation of dharmas] To say that dharmas are wholly nonexistent, denying even the existence of marks, is a wrong view. The correct view is: dharmas have marks but no essence.

Clinging to dharmas (all things) as truly existing is one erroneous extreme; clinging to dharmas as wholly nonexistent is the other erroneous extreme. What is correct is the middle way: dharmas have marks but no essence—they are illusions.

[The middle way] Neither clinging to marks nor negating marks. This is what is commonly said: not leaning toward existence nor toward non-existence; neither existence (without essence) nor non-existence (having marks); also existence (having marks) and also non-existence (without essence); not falling into either extreme, perfectly integrated and unobstructed—this is called the middle way.

In this sutra the World-Honored One, through repeated examples, clarifies this fundamental view: it is not thus (that is, not existence), and it is not otherwise (that is, not non-existence); all dharmas are illusions with marks but no essence.

The preceding section said that one must not negate the existence of marks; this section turns back and says: one must not cling to marks. With regard to the merit they produce, bodhisattvas should neither receive nor crave.

[Subhūti! If a bodhisattva were to use as a gift the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and if another person, knowing that all dharmas are without self, were to attain patient acceptance, the merit of that bodhisattva would surpass the merit of the former bodhisattva. Why is that? Subhūti! Because all bodhisattvas do not receive merit.]

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva were to use as a gift the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and if another person, knowing that all dharmas are without self, were to attain patient acceptance, the merit of that bodhisattva would surpass the merit of the former bodhisattva.”

—Subhūti! If a bodhisattva were to give as a gift the seven treasures filling the trichiliocosms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and if another bodhisattva, knowing that all dharmas are illusions, were to attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former.

[Worlds equal to the sands of the Ganges] Trichiliocosms whose number equals that of the sands of the Ganges. [Knowing that all dharmas are without self] Knowing that all dharmas have no real essence and are all illusions. [Attaining patient acceptance] Attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. “Patience” (kṣānti) means patient endurance—abiding in the principle without the mind being moved. In the Yuan Wei

Bodhiruci’s translation: “If a bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are without self and attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, this merit surpasses the merit gained earlier.” [The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas] Abbreviated as the patience of non-arising. Having realized that all dharmas are illusions, originally never having arisen and so never extinguished (neither born nor extinguished), one abides in this principle without being moved. “Patience” here means abiding—the mind abiding in the principle without wavering. In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, volume forty,
the Kaundinya chapter, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false.” The Great Commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom

volume fifty says: “The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas means that, within the true characteristic of dharmas, which neither arise nor cease, one believes, receives, and penetrates it without obstruction and without regression; this is called the patience of non-arising.”

Non-arising is the essence of the Buddha-Dharma and likewise the core of cultivation. A verse of the Pure Land school says: “When the flower opens one sees the Buddha and awakens to non-arising; the non-retreating bodhisattva is one’s companion.” The Great Commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom

seventy-three says: “In the patient acceptance of non-arising, even a subtle dharma is not obtainable, how much less a great one; this is called non-arising. Having attained this Dharma of non-arising, one does not perform or set in motion karmic actions; this is called attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. A bodhisattva who has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is called avivartika.” The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

the sixth chapter, “The Chapter on the Tongue Marks”: “At that time the Buddha knew that the good man, with utmost sincerity, in all dharmas neither arising nor ceasing, neither going forth nor acting, attained this patient acceptance of dharmas. The Buddha then smiled, and various-colored rays of light issued from his mouth. Ananda said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile? The Buddha told Ananda: In this assembly, a hundred thousand koṭis of people have attained the patient acceptance of non-arising with regard to dharmas. In a future age, after passing through six thousand eight hundred million kalpas, these people shall become Buddhas; the kalpa shall be called the Accumulation of Flowers, and the Buddhas shall all be named ‘Enlightened Flower.’”

To accomplish the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, one must not only sever the self of persons but must also sever the self of dharmas. If one cultivates while still attaching to a self of dharmas, that very mind is a mind of arising and ceasing, which cannot accomplish the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. To better comprehend the principle of non-arising, I now excerpt a passage discussing birth and death from the Direct Explanation of the True Mind:

Someone asked: I have heard that a person who sees the nature transcends birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old were people who saw the nature, and they all had birth and death. Now we see, in the present world, that those who cultivate the Way also undergo birth and death. How can they be said to transcend birth and death?

Reply: Birth and death are originally nonexistent; deluded reckoning takes them to be real. It is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky (that is, blossoms in empty space). When one without eye disease says, “There are no flowers in the sky,” the diseased person does not believe it. Once the eye disease is gone, the flowers in the sky vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe there are no flowers. While the flowers have not yet vanished, those flowers too are empty; it is only the diseased person who deludedly grasps them as flowers—they are not truly existing as a substance. It is likewise when a person deludedly takes birth and death to be real, and one who has transcended birth and death tells him, “Originally there is no birth and death.” When, one day, his delusion ceases, birth and death vanish of themselves, and only then does he know that birth and death were originally nonexistent. Even when birth and death have not yet ceased, they too are not truly real, precisely because he deludedly takes birth and death to be real. The sutra (the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment) says: ‘Good man, all sentient beings, from time without beginning, have been utterly inverted, like one who is lost and changes his direction in all four places, deludedly taking the four great elements as the characteristic of his own body and the shadows of the six sense objects as the characteristic of his own mind—like the diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky. And even as those flowers in the sky vanish in the sky, one cannot say there is a definite place where they cease. Why is that? Because there is no place of their arising. All sentient beings, within non-arising, deludedly see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called transmigrating through birth and death.’ According to this sutra text, one may be certain that, having penetrated the true mind of perfect enlightenment, originally there is no birth and death. When one now knows there is no birth and death, yet is unable to escape from birth and death, it is because the exertion is not yet sufficient. Therefore in the teachings it is said that the woman Ambapālī asked Mañjuśrī: ‘Clearly knowing that birth is the Dharma of non-arising, why is one nevertheless carried along by birth and death?’ Mañjuśrī said: ‘Because his power is not yet full.’ Later a mountain master asked the cultivator master: ‘Clearly knowing that birth is the Dharma of non-arising, why is one nevertheless carried along by birth and death?’ The cultivator said: ‘A bamboo shoot will in the end become a bamboo; but as it now stands, can one make a bamboo slat of it?’ Thus, to know there is no birth and death is not as good as to realize there is no birth and death; to realize there is no birth and death is not as good as to be in accord with there being no birth and death; and to be in accord with there being no birth and death is not as good as to employ there being no birth and death. People today do not even know there is no birth and death—how much less to realize it, be in accord with it, or employ it? So it is not fitting that those who take birth and death to be real should disbelieve in the Dharma of no birth and death!
